Surah al-Hadid is Medinan and has twenty-nine verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Allah, and He is the Almighty, the Wise.﴾ ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He gives life and causes death, and He is over all things competent.﴾ ﴿He is the First and the Last, and the Ascendant and the Intimate, and He is, of all things, Knowing.﴾ ﴿He it is who created the heavens and the earth in six days; then He established Himself above the Throne. He knows what enters into the earth and what emerges from it, what descends from the sky and what ascends into it. And He is with you wherever you are. And Allah, of what you do, is Seeing.﴾ ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and to Allah are returned all matters.﴾ ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night, and He is Knowing of what is within the breasts.﴾

Al-Naqqash and others said: this surah is Medinan by the consensus of the exegetes. Others, such as al-Zamakhshari, said: it is Meccan. Ibn 'Atiyya said: there is no disagreement that it contains Medinan Qur'an, but its opening resembles being Meccan.

The connection (munasabah) between the beginning of this surah and the end of what precedes it is clear, for He, exalted is He, commanded glorification, then informed that the glorification commanded has been performed and upheld by everyone in the heavens and the earth. The verb "sabbaha" (glorified) is in the past tense, and "yusabbihu" (glorifies) is in the present tense, and both indicate permanence and continuity, and that this is the constant practice of whoever is in the heavens and the earth. The glorification (tasbih) here, according to most, means the transcendence (tanzih) known in the phrase "subhan Allah." It was said: it is literal for all of them. It was said: it applies to those among them who are capable of glorifying. It was said: it is figurative, meaning that the trace of craftsmanship in them alerts the beholder to glorify. It was said: the glorification here is prayer (salah). Regarding inanimate objects this is far-fetched; regarding the disbeliever, the prostration of his shadow is his prayer; regarding the believer, this is acceptable. The "li" in "lillah" may either be like the "li" in "nasahtu li-Zayd" (I advised Zayd), where one says "sabbih Allah" just as one says "nasahtu Zaydan," so the "li" is brought to strengthen the arrival of the verb at its object; or it may be the "li" of causation, meaning: produce the glorification for the sake of Allah, that is, for His face, sincerely.

﴿Yuhyi wa yumit﴾ (He gives life and causes death): a independent sentence with no place in the grammatical structure relative to ﴿lahu mulku as-samawati wa al-ard﴾ (to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth). When He informed that dominion belongs to Him, He informed about His essence with these two great attributes by which complete disposal over the dominion is achieved, namely bringing into existence whatever He wills and annihilating whatever He wills; and for this reason He followed with the power by which there is giving life and causing death. It is also permitted that it be the predicate of an implied subject, meaning: He is the One who gives life and causes death; and that it be a circumstantial clause (hal), with the pronoun in "lahu" as its referent, and the governing element being that which governs the prepositional phrase.

It was said: the First is He who was before everything, and the Last is He who remains after the perishing of everything. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: the First by pre-eternity, and the Last by everlastingness. It was said: "al-Zahir" is the one who is high above everything, the one who prevails over whatever he rises above and overcomes; and "al-Batin" is the one who knows the inner reality of everything, that is, He knows its inside. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, what is the meaning of the waw (and)? I say: the first waw indicates that He combines the two attributes of firstness and lastness; the second indicates that He combines manifestness and hiddenness; and the middle one indicates that He combines the totality of the first two attributes with the totality of the latter two. So He is the one whose existence is continuous at all times, past and future, and in all of them He is manifest by proofs and hidden so that He is not perceived by the senses. (p. 218) ﴿Believe in Allah and His Messenger, and spend from that in which He has made you successors. So those among you who have believed and spent will have a great reward.﴾ ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not believe in Allah while the Messenger invites you to believe in your Lord, and He has already taken your covenant, if you are [truly] believers?﴾ ﴿It is He who sends down to His Servant clear verses to bring you out from darknesses into the light. And indeed, Allah is toward you Kind and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not spend in the way of Allah, while to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth? Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest. Those are greater in rank than those who spent afterward and fought. But to each Allah has promised the best [reward]. And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾ ﴿Who is it that would loan Allah a goodly loan so He will multiply it for him and he will have a noble reward?﴾.

When He, the Exalted, mentioned the glorification of the world for Him, and what it contains of dominion and disposal, and the lofty attributes with which He described Himself, and concluded them with His being Knower of what is concealed in the breasts, He commanded His believing servants to remain steadfast in faith, to persist in it, and to spend in the way of Allah, the Exalted. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it was revealed concerning the Battle of Tabūk.

﴿Mustakhlafīna fīh﴾ (made successors in it): meaning, it is not truly yours; rather it has passed to you from others. Just as it reached you, you will leave it for others. This contains a discouragement from what is in people's hands, since its ultimate destination is another, and they have of it only what came in the ḥadīth: "The son of Adam says, 'My wealth, my wealth.' And do you have of your wealth except what you eat and so consume, or wear and so wear out, or give in charity and so send ahead?" It was said to a Bedouin: "To whom do these camels belong?" He said: "They belong to Allah, the Exalted, in my keeping." Or the meaning may be: He, the Exalted, brought these possessions into being, then granted them to you and made you successors (khulafāʾ) in their disposal; so you are in them like agents (wukalāʾ). So spend from them in the rights of Allah, the Exalted.

Then He, the Exalted, mentioned the reward for the believer who spends, and described it as noble in order to surpass him in kinds of reward. It was said: this contains an allusion to ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān (may Allah be pleased with him), since he expended that great expenditure in the army of hardship (jaysh al-ʿusra). Then He said: ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not believe in Allah﴾, and this is a question in the manner of rebuke and denunciation: meaning, how is it that you do not remain steadfast in faith? The motives for it are present, and that is an inherent disposition in you from the proofs of reason. What necessitates it from revelation is His saying: ﴿while the Messenger invites you﴾, because of this sublime quality. The covenant concerning faith has already been taken from you, so the motives for faith are present and its causes are attained; there is no obstacle to it and no excuse for abandoning it. ﴿Lā tu'minūn﴾ (you do not believe) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), as you say: "What is with you that you do not stand?" denouncing his not standing. (*Wa-al-Rasūl*): the waw here is the waw of circumstance (wāw al-ḥāl), so the clause after it is a circumstance, and there is a third circumstance, "and He has already taken your covenant." It was said that this covenant is the one taken from them at the time of their extraction from the loins of Adam, peace be upon him. And it was said: it is the proofs set up and fixed in the intellects through reflection upon them.

﴿In kuntum mu'minīn﴾ (if you are believers): a conditional clause whose response is omitted, meaning: if you are believers for some cause, then this is the cause of your faith; or: if you are among those who believe, then what is with you that you do not believe while the situation is this, namely the Messenger's invitation and the taking of the covenant? Al-Ṭabarī said: if you are believers in any state of affairs, then now. The majority (al-Jumhūr) read ﴿wa-qad akhadha﴾ with the verb in the active voice, and (mīthāqakum) in the accusative; Abū ʿAmr read it in the passive voice, with (mīthāqakum) in the nominative. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: in His saying ﴿in kuntum mu'minīn﴾, the meaning is that His saying ﴿while the Messenger invites you to believe in your Lord, and He has already taken your covenant, if you are [truly] believers﴾ requires that it be understood in its wake, so you are in lofty ranks and elevated stations.

﴿In kuntum mu'minīn﴾: meaning, if you persist in what you have begun with.

When He mentioned the preparation for what necessitates faith, namely the Messenger's invitation to them to believe, He mentioned that He, the Exalted, is the One who sends down to His Messenger, ﷺ, what he calls to faith with, namely the clear verses and miracles, in order to bring you out from the darknesses of disbelief into the light of faith; that is, Allah, the Exalted, since He is the one who informs about it, or the Messenger, ﷺ, since he is closer. It was recited in the seven readings: (yunazzilu) in the present tense, some with doubling (tashdīd) and some without (takhfīf). The recitation of al-Ḥasan: with both forms. Zayd ibn ʿAlī and al-Aʿmash: (anzala) in the past tense. He described Himself, the Exalted, with tenderness and mercy in order to make them feel at ease.

Since He had commanded them to believe and to spend, and then abandoned rebuking them for not believing despite the presence of what necessitates it, He rebuked them for not spending in the way of Allah, while the motive for it is present, namely that they will die and leave it behind. He drew attention to this necessitating cause by His saying: ﴿while to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth﴾, and this is among the most eloquent incitements to spend. ﴿An lā tunfiqū﴾ (that you do not spend): its underlying form is "in that you do not spend," so its position is either genitive or accusative according to the grammatical disagreement (al-khilāf), and ʾan is not superfluous but is a verbal-nominal particle (maṣdariyya). Al-Akhfash said, concerning His saying ﴿wa-mā lanā allā nuqātila﴾ [al-Baqarah: 246], that it is a superfluous governing ʾan, its underlying form in his view being: "What is with us that we do not fight?" Therefore, according to his school in that verse, here ʾan would be, and its underlying form is: "What is with you that you do not spend?" But his view has been refuted in the books of grammar.

﴿Lā yastawī minkum man anfaqa min qabli al-fatḥ wa-qātala﴾ (not equal among you are those who spent before the conquest and fought): it was said: it was revealed concerning Abū Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), since he was the first to accept Islam, emigrate, and spend, may Allah be pleased with him, and likewise those who followed him in precedence in that; and for this reason He said: ﴿Those are greater in rank﴾. It was also said: it was revealed because some of the Companions spent great sums, to the point that it was said: these people have greater reward than everyone who spent. This clause contains the difference between the spenders. The majority read ﴿min qabli al-fatḥ﴾; Zayd ibn ʿAlī is said to have read it without (min). "Al-fatḥ" is the conquest of Makkah, and this is the well-known view, and the statement of Qatādah, Zayd ibn Aslam and Mujāhid. Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī and al-Shaʿbī said: it is the conquest of al-Ḥudaybiyah, and its being a conquest has already been mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Fatḥ; Abū Saʿīd traced it to the Prophet, ﷺ: "Indeed, the best of what lies between the two emigrations is the conquest of al-Ḥudaybiyah." The apparent reading is that (man) is the subject of (lā yastawī), and its counterpart has been omitted, namely "those who spent after the conquest and fought," because the meaning is clear.

(ʾUlāʾika): meaning, those who spent before the conquest and before the spread and wide diffusion of Islam and the Muslims' conquest of Umm al-Qurā, and they are the foremost first of the Emigrants and the Helpers, concerning whom the Prophet, ﷺ, said: "If one of you were to spend the equivalent of Mount Uḥud in gold, it would not reach a mudd of one of them, nor half of it." And far-fetched is the view of one who holds that the subject of (lā yastawī) is a pronoun referring to the spending, meaning: it is not equal, namely the spending itself, that is, its kind, since some of it is before the conquest and some after it; and (man anfaqa) would then be a subject (mubtada'), and (ʾulāʾika) a subject whose predicate is what follows, and the clause would be in the position of the predicate of (man). This involves dislocation of the speech and departure from the apparent meaning without a necessitating reason. Omitting the coordinated counterpart is common when the opposition indicates it, especially when the coordinated term is what the verb's form requires, which is (yastawī). The majority read (wa-kullan) in the accusative, as the first object of (waʿada). Ibn ʿĀmir and ʿAbd al-Wārith, through the route of al-Mādirī, read it in the nominative: (wa-kullun), and the apparent reading is that it is a subject (mubtada'), and the clause after it is in the position of the predicate. This was permitted by al-Farrāʾ and Hishām, and it was rejected in the Seven Readings, so it is obligatory to accept it; though other grammarians besides them restricted the omission of the pronoun that is omitted from such as (waʿada) to necessity. The poet said:

*And Khālid, our masters praise him rightfully, and do not praise him falsely.*

He means: our masters praise him. Some avoided making (waʿada) the predicate and said: (kullun) is a subject, and its underlying form is: "and those are each," and (waʿada) is a qualifying clause. But omitting the object pronoun from a clause that serves as a qualifier is more common than omitting it when the clause is a predicate, as in his saying:

*And I do not know whether distance changed them, or the length of time, or wealth they obtained.*

He means: they obtained it; so (aṣābū) is a qualifier of (mālun), and the pronoun referring back to the qualified noun has been omitted. (Al-Ḥusnā) is the feminine of (al-aḥsan), and Mujāhid and Qatādah explained it as Paradise. The promise includes that in the Hereafter, and victory and spoils in this world.

﴿And Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾: this contains promise and warning.

The discussion of a similar phrase, His saying ﴿Who is it that would loan Allah a goodly loan so He will multiply it for him﴾, grammatically (iʿrāb), recitation, and interpretation, has already been presented in Surat al-Baqarah. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: here the nominative (al-rafʿ), meaning in (yuḍāʿifuhu), is by coordination (ʿaṭf) or by severance and resumption (qaṭʿ wa-istiʾnāf). ʿĀṣim read (fa-yuḍāʿifahu) in the accusative by (fa) as an answer to the interrogative. In that there is some difficulty. Abū ʿAlī, meaning al-Fārisī, said: because the question did not fall on the loan; rather the question fell on the doer of the loan. The (fa) only puts into the accusative a verb that is linked to a verb about which a question is asked. However, this group among the readers, meaning, took it according to the meaning, as if His saying ﴿Who is it that would loan﴾ were in the position of saying: "Would anyone loan Allah so that He multiplies it?" (End of quotation.)

And what Abū ʿAlī held, that the (fa) only puts into the accusative a verb linked to a verb about which a question is asked, is not correct. Rather it is permissible when the interrogative is by its nominal particles, such as: "Who calls me so that I respond to him?" "Where is your house so that I visit you?" "When do you set out so that I accompany you?" "How are you so that I keep you company?" Here the question falls on the person of the caller, or on the place, time, or state, not on the verb. Ibn Kaysān related from the Arabs: "Where did Zayd go so that we follow him?" Likewise: "How much is your wealth so that we know it?" and "Who is your father so that we honor him?" with the accusative after (fa). The reading (fa-yuḍāʿifahu) in the accusative is a mutawātir reading, and the verb is the relative clause (ṣila) of (alladhī), (alladhī) is a qualifier of (dhā), and (dhā) is the predicate of (man). If the accusative is permissible in something like this, its permissibility in the earlier examples is more fitting, and Ibn Kaysān's report of it as transmitted from the Arabs supports that. The apparent reading is that His saying ﴿and he will have a noble reward﴾ is an addition beyond the multiplication that results from the loan; that is, and he will have, along with the multiplication, a noble reward.

(Al-Ḥusnā) is the feminine of (al-aḥsan), and Mujāhid and Qatādah explained it as Paradise. The promise includes that in the Hereafter, and victory and spoils in this world.

﴿And Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾: this contains promise and warning.

The discussion of a similar phrase, His saying ﴿Who is it that would loan Allah a goodly loan so He will multiply it for him﴾, grammatically (iʿrāb), recitation, and interpretation, has already been presented in Surat al-Baqarah. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: here the nominative (al-rafʿ), meaning in (yuḍāʿifuhu), is by coordination (ʿaṭf) or by severance and resumption (qaṭʿ wa-istiʾnāf). ʿĀṣim read (fa-yuḍāʿifahu) in the accusative by (fa) as an answer to the interrogative. In that there is some difficulty. Abū ʿAlī, meaning al-Fārisī, said: because the question did not fall on the loan; rather the question fell on the doer of the loan. The (fa) only puts into the accusative a verb that is linked to a verb about which a question is asked. However, this group among the readers, meaning, took it according to the meaning, as if His saying ﴿Who is it that would loan﴾ were in the position of saying: "Would anyone loan Allah so that He multiplies it?" (End of quotation.)

(p. 218) ﴿Believe in Allah and His Messenger, and spend from that in which He has made you successors. So those among you who have believed and spent will have a great reward.﴾ ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not believe in Allah while the Messenger invites you to believe in your Lord, and He has already taken your covenant, if you are [truly] believers?﴾ ﴿It is He who sends down to His Servant clear verses to bring you out from darknesses into the light. And indeed, Allah is toward you Kind and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not spend in the way of Allah, while to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth? Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest. Those are greater in rank than those who spent afterward and fought. But to each Allah has promised the best [reward]. And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾ ﴿Who is it that would loan Allah a goodly loan so He will multiply it for him and he will have a noble reward?﴾.

When He, the Exalted, mentioned the glorification of the world for Him, and what it contains of dominion and disposal, and the lofty attributes with which He described Himself, and concluded them with His being Knower of what is concealed in the breasts, He commanded His believing servants to remain steadfast in faith, to persist in it, and to spend in the way of Allah, the Exalted. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it was revealed concerning the Battle of Tabūk.

﴿Mustakhlafīna fīh﴾ (made successors in it): meaning, it is not truly yours; rather it has passed to you from others. Just as it reached you, you will leave it for others. This contains a discouragement from what is in people's hands, since its ultimate destination is another, and they have of it only what came in the ḥadīth: "The son of Adam says, 'My wealth, my wealth.' And do you have of your wealth except what you eat and so consume, or wear and so wear out, or give in charity and so send ahead?" It was said to a Bedouin: "To whom do these camels belong?" He said: "They belong to Allah, the Exalted, in my keeping." Or the meaning may be: He, the Exalted, brought these possessions into being, then granted them to you and made you successors (khulafāʾ) in their disposal; so you are in them like agents (wukalāʾ). So spend from them in the rights of Allah, the Exalted.

Then He, the Exalted, mentioned the reward for the believer who spends, and described it as noble in order to surpass him in kinds of reward. It was said: this contains an allusion to ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān (may Allah be pleased with him), since he expended that great expenditure in the army of hardship (jaysh al-ʿusra). Then He said: ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not believe in Allah﴾, and this is a question in the manner of rebuke and denunciation: meaning, how is it that you do not remain steadfast in faith? The motives for it are present, and that is an inherent disposition in you from the proofs of reason. What necessitates it from revelation is His saying: ﴿while the Messenger invites you﴾, because of this sublime quality. The covenant concerning faith has already been taken from you, so the motives for faith are present and its causes are attained; there is no obstacle to it and no excuse for abandoning it. ﴿Lā tu'minūn﴾ (you do not believe) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), as you say: "What is with you that you do not stand?" denouncing his not standing. (*Wa-al-Rasūl*): the waw here is the waw of circumstance (wāw al-ḥāl), so the clause after it is a circumstance, and there is a third circumstance, "and He has already taken your covenant." It was said that this covenant is the one taken from them at the time of their extraction from the loins of Adam, peace be upon him. And it was said: it is the proofs set up and fixed in the intellects through reflection upon them.

Al-Ṭabarī said: if you are believers in any state of affairs, then now. The majority (al-Jumhūr) read ﴿wa-qad akhadha﴾ with the verb in the active voice, and (mīthāqakum) in the accusative; Abū ʿAmr read it in the passive voice, with (mīthāqakum) in the nominative. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: in His saying ﴿in kuntum mu'minīn﴾, the meaning is that His saying ﴿while the Messenger invites you to believe in your Lord, and He has already taken your covenant, if you are [truly] believers﴾ requires that it be understood in its wake, so you are in lofty ranks and elevated stations.

﴿In kuntum mu'minīn﴾: meaning, if you persist in what you have begun with.

When He mentioned the preparation for what necessitates faith, namely the Messenger's invitation to them to believe, He mentioned that He, the Exalted, is the One who sends down to His Messenger, ﷺ, what he calls to faith with, namely the clear verses and miracles, in order to bring you out from the darknesses of disbelief into the light of faith; that is, Allah, the Exalted, since He is the one who informs about it, or the Messenger, ﷺ, since he is closer. It was recited in the seven readings: (yunazzilu) in the present tense, some with doubling (tashdīd) and some without (takhfīf). The recitation of al-Ḥasan: with both forms. Zayd ibn ʿAlī and al-Aʿmash: (anzala) in the past tense. He described Himself, the Exalted, with tenderness and mercy in order to make them feel at ease.

Al-Akhfash said, concerning His saying ﴿wa-mā lanā allā nuqātila﴾ [al-Baqarah: 246], that it is a superfluous governing ʾan, its underlying form in his view being: "What is with us that we do not fight?" Therefore, according to his school in that verse, here ʾan would be, and its underlying form is: "What is with you that you do not spend?" But his view has been refuted in the books of grammar.

It was also said: it was revealed because some of the Companions spent great sums, to the point that it was said: these people have greater reward than everyone who spent. This clause contains the difference between the spenders. The majority read ﴿min qabli al-fatḥ﴾; Zayd ibn ʿAlī is said to have read it without (min). Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī and al-Shaʿbī said: it is the conquest of al-Ḥudaybiyah, and its being a conquest has already been mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Fatḥ; Abū Saʿīd traced it to the Prophet, ﷺ: "Indeed, the best of what lies between the two emigrations is the conquest of al-Ḥudaybiyah." (ʾUlāʾika): meaning, those who spent before the conquest and before the spread and wide diffusion of Islam and the Muslims' conquest of Umm al-Qurā, and they are the foremost first of the Emigrants and the Helpers, concerning whom the Prophet, ﷺ, said: "If one of you were to spend the equivalent of Mount Uḥud in gold, it would not reach a mudd of one of them, nor half of it." This involves dislocation of the speech and departure from the apparent meaning without a necessitating reason. *And Khālid, our masters praise him rightfully, and do not praise him falsely.*

He means: our masters praise him. Some avoided making (waʿada) the predicate and said: (kullun) is a subject, and its underlying form is: "and those are each," and (waʿada) is a qualifying clause. Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 57, verse 12–15:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿On the Day you will see the believing men and the believing women, their light running before them and on their right hands. "Good tidings to you today: gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great triumph."﴾ ﴿On the Day the hypocritical men and the hypocritical women will say to those who believed, "Wait for us, that we may borrow from your light." It will be said, "Turn back behind you and seek light." So a wall will be set up between them with a gate; within it is mercy, and without it is torment.﴾ ﴿They will call out to them, "Were we not with you?" They will say, "Yes, but you led yourselves into temptation, and you waited, and you doubted, and false desires deceived you until the command of Allah came; and the Deceiver deceived you concerning Allah."﴾ ﴿So today no ransom will be taken from you, nor from those who disbelieved. Your refuge is the Fire; it is your protector, and wretched is the destination.﴾

The governing element of "يَوْمَ" (yawma, "on the Day") is the same as the governing element of "لَهم" (lahum, "for them"). The implied sense is: "And there is for them a noble reward, on the Day you see..." or "Remember the Day you see..." to magnify that Day. The seeing here is seeing with the eye, and the light is literal; this is the view of the majority (al-jumhur). Reports from Ibn 'Abbas and others have been transmitted on this, and that every manifestation of faith has a light, which extinguishes the light of the hypocrite, while the light of the believer remains. They differ in their light: among them is one whose light shines as far as between Makkah and San'a, and one whose light is like a tall palm tree, and one whose light illumines only what is near his feet. Among them is one who is sometimes on the verge of being extinguished and sometimes shines clearly, and this is according to the measure of their deeds. Al-Dahhak said: "light" is a metaphor for the guidance and the good pleasure in which they are. The apparent meaning is that the light goes before them, "between their hands," and is also "on their right hands," so it appears that there are two lights: a light running before them, and a light on their right; the one illumines the direction they head toward, and the other illumines what surrounds them from the directions. The majority said: the light originally is "on their right hands," and what is "between their hands" is the spreading radiance (p-221) from that light. It was said: the "ba'" (bi-) is in the sense of "'an," meaning "from their right hands," and the sense is: in all their directions. He expressed it by "right hands" to honor them. Al-Zamakhshari said: He said "between their hands and on their right hands" because the fortunate are given their books of deeds from these two directions, just as the wretched are given them from their left sides and from behind their backs. Al-Jumhur read "wa-bi-aymanihim" as the plural of "yamin"; Sahl ibn Shu'ayb al-Sahmi and Abu Haywa read it with a kasra on the hamza. This noun is conjoined to the adverbial phrase because the adverbial phrase is connected to an omitted element, meaning "being between their hands" and "being by means of their right hands."

"Bushrakumu al-yawma jannatun" (Good tidings to you today: gardens): this is a clause governed by an omitted saying; that is, the angels who receive them will say: "Gardens," meaning the entry into gardens. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "abiding therein forever" to the end of the verse is addressed to Muhammad (ﷺ), end of quote. There is no address here; rather this is an instance of iltifat (shift) from the pronoun of address in "bushrakum" to the pronoun of absence in "khalidin." Had it continued in address, the construction would have been "khalidan antum fiha." Iltifat is one of the arts of eloquence. "Yawma yaqulu" (on the Day the hypocrites will say) is a substitute for "yawma tara" (on the Day you see). It was also said that it is governed by "udhkur" (remember). Ibn 'Atiyya said: It appears to me that the governing element of it is "dhalika huwa al-fawz al-'azim" (that is the great triumph), and the coming of the sense of triumph is more majestic; as if he says: the believers triumph with mercy on the Day when the hypocrites suffer such-and-such, because a person's exaltation on the Day his enemy and opponent is humbled is more wondrous and majestic. End of quote. The apparent meaning of his words and his estimation is that "yawma" is in the accusative governed by "al-fawz," and this is not permitted, because it is a verbal noun already described before its complements were taken, so it cannot govern. If its description, which is "al-'azim," governed, it would be permitted; that is, the triumph which is great, meaning its extent is great, "on the Day they say."

"Unzurūnā" (Wait for us): that is, "intaẓirūnā," because when they preceded you to crossing the Sirat, and their lights had been extinguished, they said this. Al-Zamakhshari said: "unzurūnā" means "wait for us," because they are hurried to the Garden like flashing lightning on mounts that speed them along, while these are on foot; or it means "look at us," because when they look at them they face them with their faces, and the light is before them so they are illumined by it. End of quote. So "unzurūnā" is made to mean "unzurū ilaynā" (look toward us), but this sense of looking is not transitive in the language of the Arabs except with "ilā" (to), not by itself; it is only found transitive by itself in poetry. Zayd ibn 'Ali, Ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Talha and Hamza read "anẓirūnā" from the fourth form "anẓara," meaning "akhkhirūnā" (delay us), that is, "ij'alūnā fī ākhirikum" (place us at the end of you), and do not outpace us in such a way that you leave us behind, nor let us catch up with you.

"Naqtabis min nurikum" (that we may borrow from your light): that is, "nuṣib minhu" (may take from it) until we are illumined by it. It is said: "iqtabasa al-rajul" and "istaqbasa" (the man kindled/obtained), meaning he took a qabas (brand, ember) from another's fire.

"Qila irji'u warā'akum" (It will be said: Turn back behind you): the speaker is the believers or the angels. The apparent meaning is that "warā'akum" is governed by "irji'u." It was also said that it has no place in grammatical analysis because it is in the sense of "irji'u," as in their saying: "warā'aka awsa'u laka," meaning "return, you will find a wider place for you." "Irji'u" is an imperative of rebuke and expulsion, meaning: return to the place of standing where we were given triumph, and seek it there; or return to the world and seek light, that is, by acquiring its cause, which is faith; or withdraw from us, "fa-iltamisū nūran" (and seek light) other than this, so there is no path for you to borrowing from it. They knew that there is no light behind them, and this is only to make them despair.

"Fa-ḍuriba baynahum" (So a wall was set up between them): that is, between the believers and the hypocrites. "Bi-sūr" (with a wall): with a barrier. Ibn Zayd said: it is the A'raf. It was said: another barrier. Al-Jumhur read "fa-ḍuriba" in the passive voice; Zayd ibn 'Ali and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr read it in the active voice, meaning Allah. The saying of one who said that this wall is the eastern wall of the mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis is far-fetched; it is narrated from 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar and Ka'b al-Ahbar, but it is perhaps not authentic from them. The sur is the barrier encircling a city for protection from an enemy. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in "bāṭinihi" returns to the gate because it is nearest. It was said: it returns to the wall, and "bāṭinuhu" is the side belonging to the people of Paradise, and "ẓāhiruhu" is what adjoins it, "min qibalihi al-'adhab" (from its side is the torment).

"Yunādūnahum" (They will call out to them): a resumptive statement, meaning the hypocrites call out to the believers. "Alam nakun ma'akum" (Were we not with you?): that is, outwardly. "Qālū balā" (They said: Yes): that is, you were with us outwardly. "Wa-lakinnakum fatantum anfusakum" (But you led yourselves into temptation): that is, you exposed yourselves to temptation by your hypocrisy. "Wa-tarabbaṣtum" (and you waited): that is, with your faith, until you died in disbelief; or you waited for the believers to suffer misfortunes, as said by Qatada. "Wa-irtabtum" (and you doubted): you were in doubt about the matter of religion. "Wa-gharratkumu al-amāniyyu" (and false desires deceived you): these are the hopes, like their saying: "Muhammad will perish this year; the tribe of Quraysh will defeat him, having hired the confederates," and other such things; or the lengthening of hopes concerning the extension of lifespans. "Ḥattā jā'a amru Allāh" (until the command of Allah came): that is death in hypocrisy. "Al-Gharūr" (the Deceiver): is the Satan, by consensus. Simak ibn Harb read "al-Ghurūr," and this has been mentioned before.

"Fa-al-yawma lā yu'khadhu minkum fidyah" (So today no ransom will be taken from you): O hypocrites. The governing element of "al-yawm" is the verb negated by "lā," and in this is a proof against the one who forbade that. "Wa-lā min alladhīna kafarū" (nor from those who disbelieved): in the hadith: "Allah, exalted is He, will rebuke the disbeliever and say to him: Tell Me, if you had the equivalent of the whole world, would you ransom yourself with all of it from the torment of the Fire? He will say: Yes, my Lord. Allah, blessed and exalted, will say: I asked of you what is easier than that while you were in the loins of your father Adam, that you should not associate anything with Me, but you refused except to associate." Al-Jumhur read "lā yu'khadhu"; Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-A'raj, Ibn 'Amir and Harun from Abu 'Amr read it with the ta' (tu'khadhu), for the feminine gender of "fidyah."

"Hiya mawlākum" (It is your protector): it was said: "awlā bikum" (more fitting for you), and this is an explanation of meaning. It was their protector inasmuch as it gathers them and touches them, and it will be for you in the place of the protector. Similar to it is the saying of the poet:

"Greeting among them is a painful blow."

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that it means "it is your helper," that is, you have no helper other than it. The intent is the absolute negation of a helper, similar to their saying: "So-and-so was struck by such-and-such and sought help from despair (al-jaza')," and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿they will be relieved with water like molten brass﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]. It was also said: it will take charge of you as you took charge of the deeds of the people of the Fire in the world.

"Wa-lakinnakum fatantum anfusakum" (But you led yourselves into temptation): that is, you exposed yourselves to temptation by your hypocrisy. "Wa-tarabbaṣtum" (and you waited): that is, with your faith, until you died in disbelief; or you waited for the believers to suffer misfortunes, as said by Qatada. "Wa-irtabtum" (and you doubted): you were in doubt about the matter of religion. We have indeed made the signs clear to you, so that you may understand.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the men who give charity and the women who give charity, and who lend to God a goodly loan, it will be multiplied for them, and they will have a generous reward.﴾ ﴿And those who believe in God and His messengers, they are the truthful (al-siddiqun) and the martyrs (al-shuhada') with their Lord. For them is their reward and their light. But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs, they are the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾ ﴿Know that the life of this world is only play and amusement, adornment and boasting among you, and rivalry in wealth and children, like the rain whose vegetation pleases the disbelievers; then it dries up and you see it turning yellow, then it becomes debris. From Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud): The Companions became weary (mallat al-sahaba mallatan), so ﴿Has not the time come﴾ was revealed.

From Ibn Abbas: They were rebuked thirteen years after (the beginning of the mission).

It was also said: jesting became frequent among some of the young Companions, so it was revealed.

The majority of readers recited ﴿Alam﴾ (with the alif of interrogation); al-Hasan and Abu al-Sammal recited ﴿Alamma﴾. The majority read ﴿ya'ni﴾, the imperfect of a-na (to draw near, to have come), while al-Hasan read ﴿ya'in﴾, the imperfect of ana, also meaning "to have come." The meaning is: the time of the matter has drawn near.

﴿An takhsha'a﴾: to be calm and humble (tatma'inna wa-takhbutu). It is an act of the heart, and it becomes apparent in the limbs. In a hadith: "The first thing to be taken away from people is humility (al-khushu')."

﴿Li-dhikri Allah﴾: that is, for the sake of the remembrance of God, as in His saying: ﴿When God is mentioned, their hearts tremble﴾ [al-Anfal 8:2]. It was also said: or for God's reminding them.

The majority read ﴿wa-ma nazzala﴾ with shaddah (intensive form); Nafi' and Hafs read it without shaddah; al-Jahdari, Abu Ja'far, al-A'mash and Abu Amr, in the transmission of Yunus and Abbas from him, read it in the passive with shaddah; Abdullah read ﴿anzala﴾ with the hamzat al-naql (causative), in the active voice. The majority read ﴿wa-la yakunu﴾ with the third-person ya' (the ghaybah form), coordinated with ﴿an takhsha'a﴾. Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi Abla, Isma'il from Abu Ja'far, and, from Shayba, Ya'qub and Hamzah in one transmission from Sulaym from him, read ﴿wa-la takunu﴾ (second person), as a shift of grammatical person (iltifat), either as a prohibition or as a coordination with ﴿an takhsha'a﴾.

﴿Ka-alladhina utu al-kitaba min qablu﴾: they are the contemporaries of Musa, peace be upon him, from the Children of Israel. The believers were warned not to become like them in hardness of heart, since when they heard the Torah they would soften and humble themselves. ﴿So the term grew long for them﴾: that is, the waiting for the conquest (al-fath), or the waiting for the Resurrection. It was also said: the length of life. The majority read ﴿al-amad﴾ with a light dal, meaning the limit/extent of time; Ibn Kathir read it with the dal doubled, which is time itself, in its fullest extent.

﴿Fa-qasat qulubuhum﴾: they became hard, to the point that they were not moved toward good and obedience.

﴿Yuhyi al-ard ba'da mawtiha﴾: it appears that this is an illustration (tamthil) of the softening of hearts after their hardness, and of the effect of the remembrance of God upon them, just as rain affects the earth, so that after its barrenness it returns fertile. Likewise, hearts that had turned away return and come forward, and the effect of acts of obedience and humility appears in them.

The majority read ﴿al-mussaddiqin wa-al-mussaddiqat﴾ with the two sad doubled; Ibn Kathir, Abu Bakr, al-Mufaddal, Aban and Abu Amr in the transmission of Harun read them with the sad single; Ubayy read them with a ta' before the sad in both. The majority reading is from ṣadaqa (to give charity), and the single-sad reading is from taṣdiq (to affirm the truth): they affirmed the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, in what he conveyed from God the Exalted.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "What is ﴿wa-aqradu﴾ coordinated with?" I say: with the sense of the verb in ﴿al-mussaddiqin﴾, because the lam (in al-) means "those who" and the active participle has the meaning of "they affirmed," as though it were said: "Indeed, those who affirmed and lent..." End of quotation. He followed in this Abu Ali al-Farisi. But it is not correct that it be coordinated with ﴿al-mussaddiqin﴾, because what is coordinated with a relative clause is itself a relative clause, and here it has been separated by a coordinated element, namely His saying ﴿wa-al-mussaddiqat﴾. Nor is it correct that it be coordinated with the relative clause of the article in ﴿al-mussaddiqat﴾, because the pronouns differ: the pronoun of the feminine (al-mutasaddiqat) is feminine, while the pronoun of ﴿wa-aqradu﴾ is masculine. Therefore it is explained here by omitting the relative pronoun (al-mawsul), because what precedes it indicates it, since it is as if it were said: "and those who lent," as in his saying:

*Whoever among you satirizes the Messenger of God, or praises him and supports him, is the same.*

He means: "or whoever praises him." (Note on the verse: the grammatical sense is that the verb is elided after the relative clause in the poem.)

﴿Siddiq﴾ is among the intensive patterns (abniyat al-mubalaghah). Al-Zajjaj said: as far as I know, it comes only from a triliteral root. It was also said that it may come from a non-triliteral root, like missik, but this is not correct, because one says massaka and amsaka, so missik comes from massaka.

Others said: He described them with truthfulness and martyrdom, from His saying: ﴿that you may be witnesses over mankind﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:143].

﴿Boasting among you﴾: the reading of the majority is with tanwin and the accusative of baynakum; al-Sulami read it with an annexed genitive. ﴿Rivalry﴾ in number and in equipment, according to the custom of the Jahiliyyah. All of these are trivialities, unlike the matters of the Hereafter, which contain real and great matters. Al-Zamakhshari said: God likened the state of this world, and the swiftness of its passing away together with the small benefit of it, to a plant that the rain made grow, so that it became mature and full-grown, and the disbelievers who deny God's blessing in what He provided them of rain and vegetation were pleased with it. Then He sent a blight upon them, so it dried and turned yellow and became debris, as a punishment for their ingratitude, as He did with the people of the garden and the owner of the two gardens. End of quotation.

Ibn Atiyyah said: ﴿ka-mathali﴾ is in the nominative position as a description of what precedes. The picture of this example is that a person grows up in the lap of a kingdom or less than that, then matures, grows strong, gains wealth and children, and people gather around him. Then after that he begins to decline: he withers, weakens and sickens, and calamities befall his wealth and his religion, and he dies, and his affairs come to nothing, and his wealth passes to others, and his traces are effaced. So his matter is like rain that fell on land, and from that rain there grew a pleasing, delicate vegetation; then it dried up, meaning it became dry and yellow, then it was crushed, then it was scattered by the winds and came to nothing. End of quotation.

It was said: ﴿al-kuffar﴾ means the farmers, from kafara al-habb (he covered the seed), meaning he buried it in the earth. They were singled out for mention because they are the people of insight into vegetation and cultivation, and only one who truly marvels would be impressed by it. It was also said: it means those who disbelieve in God, because they are most intent on glorifying this world and most impressed by its beauties. ﴿Huttam﴾ (debris) is an intensive pattern, like ujab. It is also read as musfarran (with a doubled r). When He mentioned what the affair of this world comes to, namely perishing, He mentioned what is established and everlasting in the affair of the Hereafter: severe punishment, and His good pleasure, which is the cause of bliss.

And Allah does not like everyone self-deluded and boastful.﴾ ﴿Those who are stingy and enjoin upon people stinginess. And whoever turns away – indeed, Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear evidences and sent down with them the Book and the balance that people may maintain justice. Some of them have illustrated the racing in various forms. Abdullah said: "Be in the first row in battle." Anas said: "Witness the opening takbir (takbir al-ihram) along with the imam." Ali said: "Be the first to enter the mosque and the last to leave it." From this racing he derived that the earliest times of the prayers are more excellent. "Prepared" (uʿiddat): this indicates that it is created. The repetition of this in the Qur'an strengthens it, and the Sunnah is explicit on it. This refutes the Mu'tazilites (al-Muʿtazila), who say that it is now not created and will be created later.

"That" (dhālika): i.e., the promised forgiveness and Garden. "The bounty of Allah" (faḍlu llāh): His gift. "He gives it to whom He wills": and they are the believers.

"No disaster strikes" (mā aṣāba min muṣība): i.e., "of disaster," and he mentioned its verb in the masculine form, though it is permissible to use both the masculine and feminine. From the feminine usage is His saying: ﴿No nation precedes its term﴾ [al-Hijr: 5]. The word "disaster" (muṣība) indicates evil, because its common usage is that. Ibn Abbas said, in substance, that he meant the customary sense of disaster, which is its usage for evil, and he specified it by mention because it is more important for humankind. A disaster on the earth is like drought, earthquake, and crop blight; and among themselves, it is illness and death. It has been said that by "disaster" is meant all events, both good and evil. "Except in a Book" (illā fī kitāb): this is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ), i.e., written in it. "Before We bring it into being" (min qabli an nabraʾahā): i.e., before We create it. Baraʾa means "to create." The pronoun in nabraʾahā apparently refers to "disaster," since it is what is spoken of, and the mention of the earth and souls is in the sense of the place of the disaster. It has been said that it refers to the earth; it has been said that it refers to souls, as said by Ibn Abbas, Qatada and a group. Al-Mahdawi mentioned the permissibility of the pronoun referring to all that has been mentioned. Ibn Atiyya said: "All of these are sound knowledge, because the prior Book is eternal, before all of these." End of quote. "Indeed, that" (inna dhālika): i.e., all that has been mentioned occurs in the Book and its decree. "Is easy for Allah" (ʿalā llāhi yasīr): i.e., easy, though it may be difficult for the servants.

Therefore he does not grieve over what is lost, because he is not in a position to cause it to be lost. Thus He eased for him the matter of the events of this world by this, since he has settled his soul upon this belief. Ibn Abbas said: "No one is without grief and joy, but whoever is struck by a disaster and makes it patience, and whoever receives good and makes it gratitude." End of quote. He means that this is the praiseworthy one. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: no one controls himself when a harm descends upon him, nor when a benefit he obtains, so that he does not grieve or rejoice? It has been said that they were exemplars in it, so it is as if they commanded it.

End of quote. The damma on the tāʾ requires that the sentence be from the speech of Mary's mother, and the feminine tāʾ requires that it be from the speech of Allah, may He be exalted. This is frequent in the mutawatir readings. "And We sent down with them the Book" (wa-anzalnā maʿahumu l-kitāb): "al-kitāb" is a generic noun, and "maʿahum" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl muqaddara), i.e., "and We sent down the Book becoming with them," i.e., estimating its companionship with them, because the messengers and the Book were both sent down. Since the expression "maʿahum" was problematic for al-Zamakhshari, he interpreted "the messengers" differently from what we have interpreted, and said: ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers﴾, meaning the angels, to the prophets with proofs and miracles, ﴿and sent down with them the Book﴾, i.e., the revelation, ﴿and the balance﴾. It is related that Gabriel, peace be upon him, descended with the balance, gave it to Noah, and said: "Command your people to weigh with it."

"And We sent down iron" (wa-anzalnā l-ḥadīd). It has been said: Adam descended from the Garden and with him were five iron items: the anvil (al-sindān), the two tongs (al-kalbatān), the hammer (al-miqaʿa), the mallet (al-miṭraqa), and the needle. It is related: and with him were the grinding stone (al-misann) and the spade (al-misḥāt). And from the Prophet (ﷺ), "that Allah, may He be exalted, sent down four blessings from the heaven to the earth: He sent down iron, fire, water, and salt." End of quote. Most of the interpreters take "the balance" to mean justice. Ibn Zayd and others said: he meant by "the balances" the knowledge among people, and this is a part of justice.

"That people may maintain justice" (li-yaqūma n-nās bil-qisṭ): the apparent meaning is that it is a cause only for the sending down of the balance, but it is permissible that it be a cause for the sending down of the Book and the balance together, because "qisṭ" is justice in all things regarding all obligations, for it does not deviate in any of them; therefore came: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him, and the angels and those of knowledge, standing in justice﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 18].

"And We sent down iron": He expressed its bringing into existence by "sending down," as in His saying: ﴿And He sent down for you of the cattle﴾ [al-Zumar: 6]. Also, since commands and all matters and rulings are delivered from heaven, all of it was made a descent from it. Ibn Atiyya said this. The majority said: by "iron" is meant its genus among the metals. Ibn Abbas said: Adam descended from the Garden and with him were the anvil, the two tongs, and the miqaʿa.

"Wherein is great military might" (fīhi baʾsun shadīd): i.e., the weapons with which fighting is carried out, "and benefits for people" (wa-manāfiʿu lil-nās): in their interests, livelihoods and crafts; for there is no craft in which iron is not an instrument.

"And that Allah may make evident" (wa-liyaʿlama llāh): a cause for the sending down of the Book, the balance, and the iron.

"Those who support Him and His messengers" (man yanṣuruhu wa-rusulahu): by proofs and demonstrations drawn from the sent-down Book, and by establishing justice, and by what is made of implements of war for jihad in the way of Allah. Ibn Atiyya said: i.e., that He may know him existing; the change is not in the knowledge of Allah, but in this occurrence that went from non-existence to existence. His saying "bil-ghayb" (unseen) means: by what he heard of the attributes that are absent from him, so he believed in them because of the existence of the evidences for them.

When He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Whoever supports Him and His messengers﴾, He mentioned that He is independent of their support by His power and might, and that He only obligated them to jihad for the benefit of their own souls and to attain the reward that accrues to them. Ibn Atiyya said: The meaning of the verse is arranged thus: Allah, may He be exalted, informed that He sent His messengers, and sent down books and a legislated justice, and weapons with which to fight whoever is obstinate and does not follow the guidance of Allah, so no excuse remains. In the verse, on this interpretation, there is an exhortation to fighting.

"And We sent down iron": He expressed its bringing into existence by "sending down," as in His saying: ﴿And He sent down for you of the cattle﴾ [al-Zumar: 6]. Also, since commands and all matters and rulings are delivered from heaven, all of it was made a descent from it. Ibn Atiyya said this. The majority said: by "iron" is meant its genus among the metals. Ibn Abbas said: Adam descended from the Garden and with him were the anvil, the two tongs, and the miqaʿa.

"Wherein is great military might" (fīhi baʾsun shadīd): i.e., the weapons with which fighting is carried out, "and benefits for people" (wa-manāfiʿu lil-nās): in their interests, livelihoods and crafts; for there is no craft in which iron is not an instrument.

"And that Allah may make evident" (wa-liyaʿlama llāh): a cause for the sending down of the Book, the balance, and the iron.

"Those who support Him and His messengers" (man yanṣuruhu wa-rusulahu): by proofs and demonstrations drawn from the sent-down Book, and by establishing justice, and by what is made of implements of war for jihad in the way of Allah. Ibn Atiyya said: i.e., that He may know him existing; the change is not in the knowledge of Allah, but in this occurrence that went from non-existence to existence. His saying "bil-ghayb" (unseen) means: by what he heard of the attributes that are absent from him, so he believed in them because of the existence of the evidences for them.

When He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Whoever supports Him and His messengers﴾, He mentioned that He is independent of their support by His power and might, and that He only obligated them to jihad for the benefit of their own souls and to attain the reward that accrues to them. Ibn Atiyya said: The meaning of the verse is arranged thus: Allah, may He be exalted, informed that He sent His messengers, and sent down books and a legislated justice, and weapons with which to fight whoever is obstinate and does not follow the guidance of Allah, so no excuse remains. In the verse, on this interpretation, there is an exhortation to fighting.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 57, verses 21–25:**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Race one another to forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden whose width is like the width of the heaven and the earth, prepared for those who have believed in Allah and His messengers. That is the bounty of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills, and Allah is the possessor of great bounty.﴾ ﴿No disaster strikes upon the earth or among yourselves but that it is in a Book before We bring it into being. Indeed, that is easy for Allah.﴾ ﴿So that you will not despair over what has escaped you, nor exult over what He has given you. And Allah does not like everyone self-deluded and boastful.﴾ ﴿Those who are stingy and enjoin upon people stinginess. And whoever turns away – indeed, Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear evidences and sent down with them the Book and the balance that people may maintain justice. And We sent down iron, wherein is great military might and benefits for people, and that Allah may make evident those who support Him and His messengers unseen. Indeed, Allah is Strong and Exalted in Might.﴾.

When He mentioned what is in the Hereafter of forgiveness, He commanded racing towards it. The meaning: race towards the cause of forgiveness, which is faith and the performance of acts of obedience. Some of them have illustrated the racing in various forms. Abdullah said: "Be in the first row in battle." Anas said: "Witness the opening takbir (takbir al-ihram) along with the imam." Ali said: "Be the first to enter the mosque and the last to leave it." From this racing he derived that the earliest times of the prayers are more excellent. The word "race" (sabiquu) came as if they were on a racecourse, running towards a goal, competing with one another to reach it.

"Its width" (ʿardtuhā): i.e., its extent in vastness, as the poet said: "Thus one of many supplications, broad (fa-dhu duʿāʾin ʿarīd)." Or "width" is the opposite of "length." When width is described as expansive, it is known that the length is even more expansive and extended.

"Prepared" (uʿiddat): this indicates that it is created. The repetition of this in the Qur'an strengthens it, and the Sunnah is explicit on it. This refutes the Mu'tazilites (al-Muʿtazila), who say that it is now not created and will be created later.

"That" (dhālika): i.e., the promised forgiveness and Garden. "The bounty of Allah" (faḍlu llāh): His gift. "He gives it to whom He wills": and they are the believers.

"No disaster strikes" (mā aṣāba min muṣība): i.e., "of disaster," and he mentioned its verb in the masculine form, though it is permissible to use both the masculine and feminine. From the feminine usage is His saying: ﴿No nation precedes its term﴾ [al-Hijr: 5]. The word "disaster" (muṣība) indicates evil, because its common usage is that. Ibn Abbas said, in substance, that he meant the customary sense of disaster, which is its usage for evil, and he specified it by mention because it is more important for humankind. A disaster on the earth is like drought, earthquake, and crop blight; and among themselves, it is illness and death. It has been said that by "disaster" is meant all events, both good and evil. "Except in a Book" (illā fī kitāb): this is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ), i.e., written in it. "Before We bring it into being" (min qabli an nabraʾahā): i.e., before We create it. Baraʾa means "to create." The pronoun in nabraʾahā apparently refers to "disaster," since it is what is spoken of, and the mention of the earth and souls is in the sense of the place of the disaster. It has been said that it refers to the earth; it has been said that it refers to souls, as said by Ibn Abbas, Qatada and a group. Al-Mahdawi mentioned the permissibility of the pronoun referring to all that has been mentioned. Ibn Atiyya said: "All of these are sound knowledge, because the prior Book is eternal, before all of these." End of quote. "Indeed, that" (inna dhālika): i.e., all that has been mentioned occurs in the Book and its decree. "Is easy for Allah" (ʿalā llāhi yasīr): i.e., easy, though it may be difficult for the servants.

Then He made clear the wisdom in informing us of that which He did, namely the decree of that and the precedence of His judgment regarding it, and said: "So that you will not" (li-kay lā taʾsawū): i.e., you will not grieve, "over what has escaped you" (ʿalā mā fātakum), because if the servant is informed of this, he is at peace, and knows that what escaped him would not have reached him, and what reached him would not have missed him. Therefore he does not grieve over what is lost, because he is not in a position to cause it to be lost. Thus He eased for him the matter of the events of this world by this, since he has settled his soul upon this belief. It appears that the meaning of His saying: ﴿So that you will not grieve over what has escaped you﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 153] is that severe grief should not overtake one over the good that has escaped, so that discontent and lack of acceptance of what is decreed arise from it.

"Nor exult over what He has given you" (wa-lā tafraḥū bimā ātākum): that one rejoice with the joy that leads to the insolence (baṭar) forbidden in His saying: ﴿Do not exult; indeed, Allah does not love the exultant﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 76]. For grief may arise from it, and for this reason He concluded with His saying: ﴿And Allah does not love everyone self-deluded and boastful.﴾ The joy in what one has obtained of the world's trash (ḥuṭām) leads in one's soul to conceit, boasting, and arrogance over people; such is what is forbidden. As for grief over what has escaped of obedience to Allah, and joy in the favours of Allah, and thanks for them, and humility, this is recommended.

Ibn Abbas said: "No one is without grief and joy, but whoever is struck by a disaster and makes it patience, and whoever receives good and makes it gratitude." End of quote. He means that this is the praiseworthy one. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: no one controls himself when a harm descends upon him, nor when a benefit he obtains, so that he does not grieve or rejoice? I say: what is meant is grief that drives one to what distracts its owner from patience and submission to the command of Allah, and hope for the reward of the patient; and joy that is overbearing and diverts from gratitude. As for the grief that a person hardly avoids, along with submission and happiness in the blessing of Allah and acknowledgment of it with gratitude, there is no harm in it." End of quote.

The majority read "bimā ātākum" (what He has given you), i.e., "gave." Abdullah read "ūtītum" in the passive, i.e., "you were given." Abu Amr read "ātākum," i.e., "came to you."

"Those who are stingy" (alladhīna yabkhalūna): i.e., they are those who are stingy, or "those who" is a subject whose predicate is omitted in a general sense (ʿalā jihat al-ibhām), its estimate being: "are blameworthy," or "are promised punishment," or "are dispensed with." Or by supposing "I mean" (aʿnī), so it is in the position of an accusative. Or it is in the position of an accusative as an adjective for "every self-deluded," and although it is indefinite, it is somewhat specified as a kind, so it is permissible to describe it with a definite. Ibn Atiyya said: "This is the view of al-Akhfash." End of quote.

The world became great in their eyes, so they were stingy to give from it the rights of Allah, may He be exalted. And that was not enough for them until they commanded people to be stingy and encouraged them to withhold. The apparent meaning is that they actually commanded people. It has been said that they were exemplars in it, so it is as if they commanded it.

"And whoever turns away" (wa-man yatawalla): from what Allah has commanded. The majority read "fa-inna llāha huwa" (indeed Allah, He is); Nafi and Ibn Amir read it without "huwa," and likewise in the codices of Medina and Syria. Both readings are mutawatir (widely transmitted). Whoever affirms "huwa," Abu Ali al-Farisi said: it is good that it be a separator (faṣl), and he said: it is not good that it be an inceptive (ibtidāʾ), because omitting the inceptive is not permissible. End of quote. He means that in the other reading it has been omitted; and if it were an inceptive, its omission would not be permitted, because if you say: "Indeed Zayd, he is the virtuous one" and parse "huwa" as an inceptive, it is not permissible to omit it, because what follows it, "the virtuous one," is suitable to be the predicate of "inna," so no evidence remains for the omission of the connecting "huwa." Its parallel is: ﴿Those who show off﴾ [al-Māʿūn: 6]; "hum" may not be omitted, because what follows it may serve as a relative clause (ṣila), so no evidence remains for the omitted element. What Abu Ali went to is nothing, because he based that on the agreement of the two readings and the construction of one upon the other, and that is not so. Do you not see that there can be two readings in one wording, each having an interpretation differing from the other, like the reading of the one who read: "wa-llāhu aʿlamu bimā waḍaʿtu" (with a damma on the tāʾ), while the other reading is: ﴿bimā waḍaʿat﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 36] with the feminine tāʾ. The damma on the tāʾ requires that the sentence be from the speech of Mary's mother, and the feminine tāʾ requires that it be from the speech of Allah, may He be exalted. This is frequent in the mutawatir readings. Likewise, this may be an inceptive in the reading of whoever affirms it, even if it was not intended in the other reading, and each of the two constructions has a ruling in grammar specific to it.

"We certainly sent Our messengers with clear evidences" (laqad arsalnā rusulanā bil-bayyināt): the apparent meaning is that the messengers here are from among the children of Adam, and "clear evidences" are proofs and miracles.

"And We sent down with them the Book" (wa-anzalnā maʿahumu l-kitāb): "al-kitāb" is a generic noun, and "maʿahum" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl muqaddara), i.e., "and We sent down the Book becoming with them," i.e., estimating its companionship with them, because the messengers and the Book were both sent down. Since the expression "maʿahum" was problematic for al-Zamakhshari, he interpreted "the messengers" differently from what we have interpreted, and said: ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers﴾, meaning the angels, to the prophets with proofs and miracles, ﴿and sent down with them the Book﴾, i.e., the revelation, ﴿and the balance﴾. It is related that Gabriel, peace be upon him, descended with the balance, gave it to Noah, and said: "Command your people to weigh with it."

"And We sent down iron" (wa-anzalnā l-ḥadīd). It has been said: Adam descended from the Garden and with him were five iron items: the anvil (al-sindān), the two tongs (al-kalbatān), the hammer (al-miqaʿa), the mallet (al-miṭraqa), and the needle. It is related: and with him were the grinding stone (al-misann) and the spade (al-misḥāt). And from the Prophet (ﷺ), "that Allah, may He be exalted, sent down four blessings from the heaven to the earth: He sent down iron, fire, water, and salt." End of quote. Most of the interpreters take "the balance" to mean justice. Ibn Zayd and others said: he meant by "the balances" the knowledge among people, and this is a part of justice.

"That people may maintain justice" (li-yaqūma n-nās bil-qisṭ): the apparent meaning is that it is a cause only for the sending down of the balance, but it is permissible that it be a cause for the sending down of the Book and the balance together, because "qisṭ" is justice in all things regarding all obligations, for it does not deviate in any of them; therefore came: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him, and the angels and those of knowledge, standing in justice﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 18].

"And We sent down iron": He expressed its bringing into existence by "sending down," as in His saying: ﴿And He sent down for you of the cattle﴾ [al-Zumar: 6]. Also, since commands and all matters and rulings are delivered from heaven, all of it was made a descent from it. Ibn Atiyya said this. The majority said: by "iron" is meant its genus among the metals. Ibn Abbas said: Adam descended from the Garden and with him were the anvil, the two tongs, and the miqaʿa.

"Wherein is great military might" (fīhi baʾsun shadīd): i.e., the weapons with which fighting is carried out, "and benefits for people" (wa-manāfiʿu lil-nās): in their interests, livelihoods and crafts; for there is no craft in which iron is not an instrument.

"And that Allah may make evident" (wa-liyaʿlama llāh): a cause for the sending down of the Book, the balance, and the iron.

"Those who support Him and His messengers" (man yanṣuruhu wa-rusulahu): by proofs and demonstrations drawn from the sent-down Book, and by establishing justice, and by what is made of implements of war for jihad in the way of Allah. Ibn Atiyya said: i.e., that He may know him existing; the change is not in the knowledge of Allah, but in this occurrence that went from non-existence to existence. His saying "bil-ghayb" (unseen) means: by what he heard of the attributes that are absent from him, so he believed in them because of the existence of the evidences for them.

When He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Whoever supports Him and His messengers﴾, He mentioned that He is independent of their support by His power and might, and that He only obligated them to jihad for the benefit of their own souls and to attain the reward that accrues to them. Ibn Atiyya said: The meaning of the verse is arranged thus: Allah, may He be exalted, informed that He sent His messengers, and sent down books and a legislated justice, and weapons with which to fight whoever is obstinate and does not follow the guidance of Allah, so no excuse remains. In the verse, on this interpretation, there is an exhortation to fighting.
