Abu Hayyan's commentary on Surah 57, verses 26–29:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And We certainly sent Noah and Abraham, and We placed in their offspring prophethood and the Book. Among them is one who is guided, but many of them are defiant sinners.﴾ ﴿Then We followed in their footsteps with Our messengers, and We followed up with Jesus, son of Mary, and We gave him the Injil, and We placed in the hearts of those who followed him compassion and mercy, and monasticism which they invented; We did not prescribe it for them, but (they did it) seeking the pleasure of Allah. Yet they did not observe it with its proper observance. So We gave those of them who believed their reward, but many of them are defiant sinners.﴾ ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah and believe in His Messenger. He will give you a double portion of His mercy, and will make for you a light by which you walk, and will forgive you. Allah is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿So that the People of the Book may know that they have no power over anything of Allah's bounty, and that bounty is in the hand of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills. Allah is the Owner of great bounty.﴾

When the Exalted mentioned the sending of the messengers in general, He singled out Noah and Abraham, peace be upon them both, in this verse, honouring them by mention. As for Noah, it is because he was the first messenger to those on earth. As for Abraham, it is because most of the prophets, peace be upon them, trace their lineage to him, and he is revered in all the religious laws. Then He mentioned the most noble thing that came to their offspring, which is prophethood, through which people are guided away from misguidance; and (the Book), which refers to the four books: the Torah, the Psalms, the Gospel and the Qur'an. All of them are among the offspring of Abraham, peace be upon him, and Abraham is among the offspring of Noah, so it is correct that they are in the offspring of both of them.

In the Mushaf of Abdullah (the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, the Mushaf being the written copy of the Qur'an), the word al-nubuwwah is written with a yā' instead of a wāw, i.e. as النُّبِيَّةَ. [p. 228] Ibn Abbas said: "(And the Book)" means writing with the pen. Apparently the pronoun in مِنهم refers to the offspring. It has also been said that it refers to those to whom the messengers were sent, because the mention of sending and of messengers indicates them. With the sending of messengers, the revelation of books, and the removal of excuses by these means, they divided into one who is guided and one who is defiant, and He reported defiance of many of them.

﴿Then We followed﴾: i.e., We made them follow, and made them come after those who had gone before. ﴿in their footsteps﴾: i.e., the footsteps of the offspring. (With Our messengers): these are the messengers who came after the offspring. ﴿and We followed up with Jesus﴾: He mentioned him to honour him, and because of the spread of his community; and He attributed him to his mother, as is customary when speaking of him. The reading of al-Hasan, الأنجيل with a fatḥa on the hamza at the beginning of Surah Āl ʿImrān, has already been mentioned. Abu al-Fath said: "It is a pattern with no parallel." End of quote. It is a non-Arabic word, so it is not required that it conform to the patterns of Arabic words. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Its matter is easier than that of al-Birṭīl," meaning that it is with a fatḥa on the bāʾ (البِرْطِيل, bribe), and it seems to be Arabic; but al-Injil is non-Arabic.

It was read as رَآفَةً on the pattern فَعالَةٍ (fa‘ālah). (And We placed): it may mean "and We created", as in His words ﴿And He made the darknesses and the light﴾ [al-Anʿām: 1]; and it may mean "We made", in which case ﴿in the hearts﴾ is in the position of the second object of جَعَلْنا (ja‘alnā, "We placed"). (And monasticism) is conjoined to what precedes it, so it is included in the sentences. (They invented it): this sentence is in the position of an adjective for (monasticism). Monasticism was singled out for invention, because compassion and mercy in the heart are not acquired by a person, unlike monasticism, which consists of bodily acts together with something in the heart, so there is room for acquisition in it.

Qatada said: compassion and mercy are from Allah, while monasticism is what they invented. Monasticism is abandoning the world and its desires, including women and others, and taking up monastic cells. Abu ʿAli al-Fārisī made (and monasticism) a separate clause, cut off from the conjunction with what precedes it, "compassion and mercy". So according to him (monasticism) is in the accusative by a verb understood, explained by what follows it, and this is the category of ishtighāl (a construction where the object is governed by a verb supplied with the pronoun), meaning: "and they invented a monasticism which they invented." Al-Zamakhshari followed him and said: "Its accusative is by a hidden verb explained by the apparent one; its estimate is: 'and they invented a monasticism which they invented,' meaning they created it from themselves and abandoned it." End of quote. This is the grammatical analysis of the Mu'tazila, and Abu ʿAli was a Mu'tazili. They say: what was created by Allah is not created by the servant. So compassion and mercy are of Allah's creation, while monasticism is an innovation of the human being, so it is created by him. This parsing that they hold is not sound from the standpoint of Arabic grammar, because this kind of construction permits the nominative by the inchoative. It is not permissible to begin here with (monasticism) being indefinite, because it has no justification among the things that justify beginning with an indefinite noun.

It has been related regarding their innovation of monasticism that they split into three groups. One group fought the kings for the sake of the religion and was defeated and killed; another group sat in the cities calling people to the religion and explaining it, and did not fight, so the kings seized them and sawed them apart with saws, and they were killed; and another group went out into the wilderness, built cells and monasteries, and asked to be left in peace on condition that they withdraw, so they were left alone. Monasticism is the act attributed to monks, and the monk is the one who fears, formed on the pattern فُعْلانٌ from رَهِبَ, like خَشْيانُ from خَشِيَ. It was also read رُهْبانِيَّةً with a ḍamma. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is as if it were a nisbah (adjective of relation) to al-Ruhban, the plural of rāhib, like rākib and Rukbān." End of quote. The more appropriate view is that it is a nisbah to rahbān, and the vowel of the ra' was changed to a ḍamma, because the nisbah is a domain of change. If it were a nisbah to ruhbān as a plural, it would be returned to its singular, and it would be said rāhibiyyah; unless it has become like a proper name, in which case it is attributed to its form, as in al-Anṣār.

The apparent meaning of ﴿except seeking the pleasure of﴾ Allah is an exception that is connected, from what is an object of purpose (maf‘ūl min ajlih). The meaning becomes: He prescribed it for them seeking His good pleasure. This is the view of Mujahid, and in this case kataba (prescribed) means qaḍā (decreed). Qatada and a group said: the meaning is that He did not impose it on them, but they did it seeking the pleasure of Allah. The exception according to this is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿ), meaning: rather, they invented it seeking the pleasure of Allah.

The apparent meaning of the pronoun in (raʿawhā, "they observed it") refers to what it referred to in (ibtada‘ūhā, "they invented it"), which is the pronoun of ﴿those who followed him﴾; that is, they did not observe it as is required of one who vows to observe his vow, because it is a covenant with Allah that it is not permissible to break. Ibn Zayd said something similar: he said: "They did not persist in it, and did not fulfil its right, but changed and altered it." On the assumption that some among them did observe it, the meaning is: "they did not all observe it." Ibn Abbas and others said: the pronoun refers to the kings who fought them and expelled them. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and others said: the pronoun refers to the later generations who came after those who invented it.

﴿So We gave those who believed﴾: they are the people of compassion and mercy who followed Jesus, peace be upon him.

﴿But many of them are defiant sinners﴾: they are those who did not observe it.

﴿O you who believe﴾: the apparent meaning is that it is an address to those among the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) who believed, so the meaning of āmanū (believe) is: remain and persist. This is the meaning in every command where the one commanded is already engaged in what he is commanded to do.

﴿He will give you a double portion (kiflayn)﴾. Abu Musa al-Ashʿari said: "kiflayn means two portions in the language of Abyssinia." End of quote. The meaning is that He will give you the like of what He promised those among the People of the Book who believed, of the double portion in His words: ﴿Those will be given their reward twice﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 54], since you are like them in the two beliefs, and you do not differentiate between any of His messengers. It has been related that the believers among the People of the Book boasted over other believers that they would be given their reward twice, and claimed superiority over them, so this verse was revealed. It has also been said: the address is directed to those among the People of the Book who believed, so the meaning is: O you who believed in Moses and Jesus, believe in Muhammad (ﷺ), and Allah will give you a double portion, i.e., two shares of His mercy, because of your belief in Muhammad (ﷺ) and your belief in those before him among the messengers.

﴿And He will make for you a light by which you walk﴾: this is the light mentioned in His words: ﴿Their light runs before them﴾ [al-Ḥadīd: 12]. ﴿And will forgive you﴾: what you committed of disbelief and sins. This meaning is supported by what is established in the Ṣaḥīḥ: "Three will be given their reward twice: a man from the People of the Book who believed in his prophet and believed in me..." (the hadith).

[This is] so that the People of the Book who did not embrace Islam may know that they will not obtain anything of what has been mentioned of His bounty, namely the double portion, the light, and the forgiveness, because they did not believe in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so their belief in those before him did not benefit them, and it never earned them any merit at all. When the address is to the believers of this community and the command is for them, it has been related that when this promise to them was revealed, the People of the Book envied them, and the Jews used to magnify their religion and themselves, and claimed that they were the beloved of Allah and the people of His good pleasure. So this verse was revealed, informing them that Allah did this and made it known, ﴿so that the People of the Book may know that they are not as they claim﴾.

The majority read ﴿so that (li’allā) he may know﴾, with lā being extra, as in His words: (mā manaʿaka an lā tasjudū, "What prevented you from not prostrating") and in His words ﴿that they will not return﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 95] in some interpretations. Khaṭṭāb ibn ʿAbd Allah read: li-an lā yaʿlam. ʿAbd Allah, Ibn Abbas, ʿIkrimah, al-Jaḥdarī and ʿAbd Allah ibn Salamah read li-yaʿlam, with variations. Al-Jaḥdarī read: li-yayya yaʿlam, whose origin is li-an yaʿlam; the hamza was changed to yā' because of the kasra before it, and the nūn was assimilated into the yā' without ghunnah (nasalization), like the recitation of Khalaf: an yaḍriba without ghunnah. Then He mentioned the most noble thing that came to their offspring, which is prophethood, through which people are guided away from misguidance; and (the Book), which refers to the four books: the Torah, the Psalms, the Gospel and the Qur'an. All of them are among the offspring of Abraham, peace be upon him, and Abraham is among the offspring of Noah, so it is correct that they are in the offspring of both of them.

In the Mushaf of Abdullah (the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, the Mushaf being the written copy of the Qur'an), the word al-nubuwwah is written with a yā' instead of a wāw, i.e. as النُّبِيَّةَ. [p. 228] Ibn Abbas said: "(And the Book)" means writing with the pen. Apparently the pronoun in مِنهم refers to the offspring. It has also been said that it refers to those to whom the messengers were sent, because the mention of sending and of messengers indicates them. With the sending of messengers, the revelation of books, and the removal of excuses by these means, they divided into one who is guided and one who is defiant, and He reported defiance of many of them.

﴿Then We followed﴾: i.e., We made them follow, and made them come after those who had gone before. ﴿in their footsteps﴾: i.e., the footsteps of the offspring. (With Our messengers): these are the messengers who came after the offspring. ﴿and We followed up with Jesus﴾: He mentioned him to honour him, and because of the spread of his community; and He attributed him to his mother, as is customary when speaking of him. The reading of al-Hasan, الأنجيل with a fatḥa on the hamza at the beginning of Surah Āl ʿImrān, has already been mentioned. Abu al-Fath said: "It is a pattern with no parallel." End of quote. It is a non-Arabic word, so it is not required that it conform to the patterns of Arabic words. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Its matter is easier than that of al-Birṭīl," meaning that it is with a fatḥa on the bāʾ (البِرْطِيل, bribe), and it seems to be Arabic; but al-Injil is non-Arabic.

It was read as رَآفَةً on the pattern فَعالَةٍ (fa‘ālah). (And We placed): it may mean "and We created", as in His words ﴿And He made the darknesses and the light﴾ [al-Anʿām: 1]; and it may mean "We made", in which case ﴿in the hearts﴾ is in the position of the second object of جَعَلْنا (ja‘alnā, "We placed"). (And monasticism) is conjoined to what precedes it, so it is included in the sentences. (They invented it): this sentence is in the position of an adjective for (monasticism). Monasticism was singled out for invention, because compassion and mercy in the heart are not acquired by a person, unlike monasticism, which consists of bodily acts together with something in the heart, so there is room for acquisition in it.

Qatada said: compassion and mercy are from Allah, while monasticism is what they invented. Monasticism is abandoning the world and its desires, including women and others, and taking up monastic cells. Abu ʿAli al-Fārisī made (and monasticism) a separate clause, cut off from the conjunction with what precedes it, "compassion and mercy". So according to him (monasticism) is in the accusative by a verb understood, explained by what follows it, and this is the category of ishtighāl (a construction where the object is governed by a verb supplied with the pronoun), meaning: "and they invented a monasticism which they invented." Al-Zamakhshari followed him and said: "Its accusative is by a hidden verb explained by the apparent one; its estimate is: 'and they invented a monasticism which they invented,' meaning they created it from themselves and abandoned it." End of quote. This is the grammatical analysis of the Mu'tazila, and Abu ʿAli was a Mu'tazili. They say: what was created by Allah is not created by the servant. So compassion and mercy are of Allah's creation, while monasticism is an innovation of the human being, so it is created by him. This parsing that they hold is not sound from the standpoint of Arabic grammar, because this kind of construction permits the nominative by the inchoative. It is not permissible to begin here with (monasticism) being indefinite, because it has no justification among the things that justify beginning with an indefinite noun.

It has been related regarding their innovation of monasticism that they split into three groups. One group fought the kings for the sake of the religion and was defeated and killed; another group sat in the cities calling people to the religion and explaining it, and did not fight, so the kings seized them and sawed them apart with saws, and they were killed; and another group went out into the wilderness, built cells and monasteries, and asked to be left in peace on condition that they withdraw, so they were left alone. Monasticism is the act attributed to monks, and the monk is the one who fears, formed on the pattern فُعْلانٌ from رَهِبَ, like خَشْيانُ from خَشِيَ. It was also read رُهْبانِيَّةً with a ḍamma. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is as if it were a nisbah (adjective of relation) to al-Ruhban, the plural of rāhib, like rākib and Rukbān." End of quote. The more appropriate view is that it is a nisbah to rahbān, and the vowel of the ra' was changed to a ḍamma, because the nisbah is a domain of change. If it were a nisbah to ruhbān as a plural, it would be returned to its singular, and it would be said rāhibiyyah; unless it has become like a proper name, in which case it is attributed to its form, as in al-Anṣār.

The apparent meaning of ﴿except seeking the pleasure of﴾ Allah is an exception that is connected, from what is an object of purpose (maf‘ūl min ajlih). The meaning becomes: He prescribed it for them seeking His good pleasure. This is the view of Mujahid, and in this case kataba (prescribed) means qaḍā (decreed). Qatada and a group said: the meaning is that He did not impose it on them, but they did it seeking the pleasure of Allah. The exception according to this is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿ), meaning: rather, they invented it seeking the pleasure of Allah.

The apparent meaning of the pronoun in (raʿawhā, "they observed it") refers to what it referred to in (ibtada‘ūhā, "they invented it"), which is the pronoun of ﴿those who followed him﴾; that is, they did not observe it as is required of one who vows to observe his vow, because it is a covenant with Allah that it is not permissible to break. Ibn Zayd said something similar: he said: "They did not persist in it, and did not fulfil its right, but changed and altered it." On the assumption that some among them did observe it, the meaning is: "they did not all observe it." Ibn Abbas and others said: the pronoun refers to the kings who fought them and expelled them. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and others said: the pronoun refers to the later generations who came after those who invented it.

﴿So We gave those who believed﴾: they are the people of compassion and mercy who followed Jesus, peace be upon him.

﴿But many of them are defiant sinners﴾: they are those who did not observe it.

﴿O you who believe﴾: the apparent meaning is that it is an address to those among the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) who believed, so the meaning of āmanū (believe) is: remain and persist. This is the meaning in every command where the one commanded is already engaged in what he is commanded to do.

﴿He will give you a double portion (kiflayn)﴾. Abu Musa al-Ashʿari said: "kiflayn means two portions in the language of Abyssinia." End of quote. The meaning is that He will give you the like of what He promised those among the People of the Book who believed, of the double portion in His words: ﴿Those will be given their reward twice﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 54], since you are like them in the two beliefs, and you do not differentiate between any of His messengers. It has been related that the believers among the People of the Book boasted over other believers that they would be given their reward twice, and claimed superiority over them, so this verse was revealed. It has also been said: the address is directed to those among the People of the Book who believed, so the meaning is: O you who believed in Moses and Jesus, believe in Muhammad (ﷺ), and Allah will give you a double portion, i.e., two shares of His mercy, because of your belief in Muhammad (ﷺ) and your belief in those before him among the messengers.

﴿And He will make for you a light by which you walk﴾: this is the light mentioned in His words: ﴿Their light runs before them﴾ [al-Ḥadīd: 12]. ﴿And will forgive you﴾: what you committed of disbelief and sins. This meaning is supported by what is established in the Ṣaḥīḥ: "Three will be given their reward twice: a man from the People of the Book who believed in his prophet and believed in me..." (the hadith).

[This is] so that the People of the Book who did not embrace Islam may know that they will not obtain anything of what has been mentioned of His bounty, namely the double portion, the light, and the forgiveness, because they did not believe in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so their belief in those before him did not benefit them, and it never earned them any merit at all. When the address is to the believers of this community and the command is for them, it has been related that when this promise to them was revealed, the People of the Book envied them, and the Jews used to magnify their religion and themselves, and claimed that they were the beloved of Allah and the people of His good pleasure. So this verse was revealed, informing them that Allah did this and made it known, ﴿so that the People of the Book may know that they are not as they claim﴾.

The majority read ﴿so that (li’allā) he may know﴾, with lā being extra, as in His words: (mā manaʿaka an lā tasjudū, "What prevented you from not prostrating") and in His words ﴿that they will not return﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 95] in some interpretations. Khaṭṭāb ibn ʿAbd Allah read: li-an lā yaʿlam. ʿAbd Allah, Ibn Abbas, ʿIkrimah, al-Jaḥdarī and ʿAbd Allah ibn Salamah read li-yaʿlam, with variations. Al-Jaḥdarī read: li-yayya yaʿlam, whose origin is li-an yaʿlam; the hamza was changed to yā' because of the kasra before it, and the nūn was assimilated into the yā' without ghunnah (nasalization), like the recitation of Khalaf: an yaḍriba without ghunnah. Ibn Mujahid related from al-Ḥasan: laylā, like Laylā, the name of a woman, with yaʿlamu with a ḍamma on the mīm; its origin is la-an lā with a fatḥa on the lām of the preposition, which is a dialect. The hamza was dropped by an irregular elision, and the nūn was assimilated into the lām, so the similar letters came together and the pronunciation became heavy, so they replaced the quiescent letter with a yā', and it became laylā. The mīm was given a ḍamma because in is here the light form of the heavy (an, i.e. the lightened ʾinna), not the one that governs the imperfect, since the original is: la-annahu lā yaʿlamu.

Quṭrub, also from al-Ḥasan: li’allā with a kasra on the lām; its explanation is like the previous one, except that he gave the lām a kasra according to the well-known dialect of the lām of the preposition. From Ibn Abbas: kay yaʿlam, and from him: li-kaylā yaʿlam; from ʿAbd Allah, Ibn Jubayr and ʿIkrimah: li-kay yaʿlam.

The majority read: an lā yaqdirūna ʿalā shay’ with the nūn, so an is the lightened form of the heavy (an); ʿAbd Allah read it with its omission, so an is the one governing the imperfect. And Allah knows best.
